archetype.name: Pocket Passer (play-action distributor)
archetype.definition: A timing-and-rhythm thrower who wins from the pocket by hitting intermediate windows off a run-leaning scheme, contributes nothing as a runner, and lives or dies on protection and the players around him.

report.headline: The intermediate passing carried the first half; the last three games have gone flat.
report.take:
Goff is who he has been for four years in Detroit: a pocket thrower who turns a well-built offense into efficient passing. At 0.229 EPA per dropback (8th of 49) and 266.8 yards a game (5th), he sits 0.232 EPA per dropback above the qualifier average. That lines up with his 2022-2025 run, when he was a top-16 EPA passer every year. He has no legs to speak of: 20 rushing yards, -0.8 EPA per carry, six scrambles with no first downs. Everything he adds comes from the arm.

What is different this year is where the value comes from. He is more aggressive into tight windows than last season (16.85% against 12.5%) and throws to an 8.06-yard intended depth, deeper than the 6.8 aDOT he posted the last two years. It has paid off. Throws of 10+ air yards produced 73.3 EPA, more than all of his dropbacks combined (60), and the 10-19 band alone ran at 0.737 per attempt. Everything short, including screens and checkdowns, has been fine but ordinary. Behind the line it is a net negative (-0.078), and Gibbs as a receiver barely moves the needle (0.018 EPA per target). LaPorta (0.679 per target) and Jameson Williams (0.538) are the ones turning his aggression into points.

The numbers hide how much the last three games have flattened. Detroit went 3-0 in Weeks 7-9, but Goff's EPA per dropback fell to 0.018, his TD rate to 3.7% and his sack rate rose to 8.9%. He threw two interceptions after none in the first five games. The aggressiveness that drove the early season vanished: 4% against Minnesota and 0% against Miami, with intended air yards of 6.0 and 6.9. Minnesota is the league's top defense, so that game is forgivable. Miami ranks 32nd, so that one is not. With a team that already passes 4.2 points less than expected, the Lions sat on leads and played field position. That shows in three straight unders after five straight overs.

Two things look shakier than the headline numbers. Third down has been bad all year: -0.222 EPA, an -11.3 CPOE and 8 of his 19 sacks, facing 7.3 yards to go on average. And a 0.7% interception rate is out of character for a passer who threw 12 picks in both 2023 and 2024. Expect the early-season peak to settle back. But this is still a top-10 efficiency passer, and the recent dip looks more like a conservative plan and a tougher stretch than a decline in his throwing.

strengths.title: Intermediate windows drive everything
strengths.body: The 10-19 yard throws are the engine: 67 attempts at 0.737 EPA with a 61.2% success rate. That is crossers and in-breakers off play-action to LaPorta, Williams and St. Brown. It is a repeatable, scheme-supported skill he showed in 2024. The rate will cool, but the area stays a strength.

strengths.title: More aggressive than his norm
strengths.body: He is throwing into tight coverage more than at any point in his Detroit tenure. That pushes his intended depth above the short-area profile of recent years. The deep sample is only 22 attempts, and a 13.1 CPOE on them will not hold. The willingness to push the ball is what separates his good games from his ordinary ones.

strengths.title: Efficiency well above league
strengths.body: His adjusted net yards per dropback (8.47) sits 1.8 above the qualifier average. He ranks 6th in passing EPA per game. A ten-year track record says this level is real rather than a hot start.

concerns.title: Third down is a problem
concerns.body: On third down he has been a liability: -0.222 EPA, a 33.3% conversion rate and an -11.3 CPOE. Eight sacks came there. Long distances are part of it, at 7.3 yards to go, and a run-first offense tends to create those. Still, holding the ball into obvious passing downs is a pattern worth watching, especially with his starting-level center out.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He is pressured on only 17.6% of dropbacks, 11th-lowest, but 31.4% of that pressure becomes a sack (27th of 42). He was around a quarter the last two seasons. This is not the price of extending plays, because he barely scrambles. It reads as holding the ball (time to throw is up 0.14 seconds) while waiting on deeper concepts. Some of it should normalize, but it is the cost of the new aggressiveness.

concerns.title: Recent slide and INT luck
concerns.body: The last three games averaged 0.018 EPA per dropback with a 2.4% interception rate. That rate is far closer to his career norm than the season's 0.7%. Two of those games came against top-10 defenses. The Miami dud, with zero aggressive throws, suggests a deliberately conservative plan more than a real decline. Even so, the turnover-free stretch is over.

trend.note: He topped 9 passing EPA in five of his first six games. Then he posted -4.2 against Minnesota and -3.4 against Miami, with his aggressiveness dropping to nearly zero, even as Detroit kept winning low-scoring games.

nextGame.headline: A leaky downfield defense, at home, in a projected shootout
nextGame.body:
New England is the kind of defense that suits what Goff does best. It ranks 24th against the pass, 28th in deep-pass EPA allowed and 29th in explosive-pass rate. It also gives the most EPA per target in the league to opposing WR1s and the second-most to WR2s. That points the ball toward St. Brown and Williams on the in-breakers and shots that drove his early season. The catch is the pass rush: New England's sack rate ranks 5th. That presses on his worst trait, turning pressure into sacks, and on his third-down problems. The Book's 51.5 total and Detroit's 30th-ranked defense suggest he will be asked to throw more than in the last three weeks.

Availability tilts his way in the secondary. Corner Charles Woods (44% of snaps) is out and Carlton Davis III (87%) is questionable with a knee. Losing Davis would thin a coverage group that already struggles against outside receivers. On his side, center Cade Mays (66% of snaps) is out, which weakens the interior protection against a defense that gets home. New England's offense ranks 9th in pass EPA but is without A.J. Brown and Henderson, with Stevenson questionable. That may lower the shootout ceiling a little.

keyMatchups.title: Outside receivers vs a weak secondary
keyMatchups.body: New England allows 0.83 EPA per target to WR1s, the worst mark in the league, and 0.61 to WR2s. St. Brown has 86 targets and Williams has been hugely efficient. With Woods out and Davis questionable, the boundary is where Goff should attack.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots against a soft shell
keyMatchups.body: The Patriots rank 28th in deep EPA allowed, giving up 1.004 per play. Goff's own deep numbers are excellent on a small sample. If the aggressiveness comes back, this is the matchup to show it.

keyMatchups.title: Pass rush vs a patched interior
keyMatchups.body: New England's 7.7% sack rate ranks 5th. Goff converts pressure to sacks at a bottom-third rate, and Mays is out at center. Sacks on third down are the most likely way this matchup goes sideways.

nextGame.watch: Whether his aggressive-throw rate rebounds from the near-zero of the last two games. If it does, the intermediate and deep game should eat against this secondary.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable. He has a strong supporting cast and a scheme that manufactures intermediate windows, and he has been a top-16 EPA passer for four straight years. Expect him to finish as a top-10 efficiency quarterback, though below his early-season peak. Two things will regress. His 0.7% interception rate should drift toward his usual 8-12 a season, so plan on roughly a pick every other game. And the deep CPOE on 22 attempts will cool. His pressure-to-sack rate should ease toward his recent norm, which would help on third down.

Volume is the swing variable. Detroit passes less than expected, and when it leads it has shown it will shrink his role to about 25 attempts. A 30th-ranked defense, though, should keep forcing shootouts like the early-season overs. Pacheco is on IR until late December and Saylors is out, so the backfield is thin behind Gibbs. That could push a bit more weight onto the passing game.
swingFactors: Whether the aggressive downfield approach returns or the conservative Weeks 8-9 plan sticks
How often Detroit's 30th-ranked defense forces him into shootouts

confidence.note: An eight-game sample and a long, stable career baseline, but the recent three-game drop has no clear injury or role cause.
